independent_variables.name: EFF
independent_variables.definition: Negative of the average number of firms followed by the focal firm’s analysts in a year: sum the number of firms covered by those analysts and divide by the number of analysts covering the focal firm. The negative sign makes higher EFF represent greater effort. It is not percentage-scaled.
independent_variables.formula: −[sum of firms followed by the focal firm’s analysts / number of analysts covering the focal firm]

evidence.quote: We define EFF as the negative of the average number of firms followed by the firm’s analysts, i.e., the sum of the number of firms covered by a firm’s analysts in a particular year divided by the number of analysts covering the firm in that year.
We multiply the average number of firms by −1 so that EFF is increasing in effort.
EFF = Negative of the average number of firms covered by the firm’s analysts.

research_interest_evidence.quote: we include in (1) our proxy for analyst effort, EFF

independent_variables.name: RESAVP_P
independent_variables.definition: Separate regressor for the positive portion/category of RESAVP. RESAVP is VDIF less the fitted value from the regression on the intangible-asset proxies, equivalently the intercept plus residual from equation (A2). The table scales RESAVP terms as percentages; the precise sign-split coding and treatment of zero are not reported.

evidence.quote: In the regression estimations we permit different coefficients on positive and negative RESAVP,

The proxy for mispricing that we include in our hypothesis tests, RESAVP, is the residual from this regression plus the intercept and, thus, the portion of analysts’ perceived mispricing that is orthogonal to our accounting proxies.

Our proxy for residual mispricing, RESAVP, equals VDIF minus the predicted VDIF based on the intangibles proxies, i.e., the sum of the intercept and estimated residual from the untabulated regression in (A2), α ˆ0 + ε ˆ A 2.
All variables except for COV, EFF, MV, BROKER, and VOL are expressed as percentages.

independent_variables.name: GROWTH
independent_variables.definition: Sales-growth proxy. Table 4 gives a ratio-to-the-power-1/i definition with 3≤i≤5 and says the variable is expressed as a percentage. Page 10 describes the five-year version with a −1 and says to use four or three years if five-year history is unavailable; that detailed formula conflicts with Table 4’s formula, which omits −1. The selected Table 4 specification is recorded in formula, while the conflict remains unresolved.

evidence.quote: growth, measured as (sales t −1 / sales t −6) <sup>1</sup> <sup>/</sup> <sup>5</sup> - 1, where year t is the current
If a firm does not have available data from five years prior to year t, we compute sales growth over four or three years, if available.
GROWTH = (sales t −1 / sales t −(1+ i )) <sup>1</sup> <sup>/i</sup> , where 3 ≤ i ≤ 5 .
All variables except for COV, EFF, MV, BROKER, and VOL are expressed as percentages.

research_interest_evidence.quote: Equation (1) includes controls for size and growth based on prior analyst coverage research
Thus, including GROWTH in the estimation equation helps ensure our findings are not attributable to correlation between growth and our accounting proxies.

dependent_variable.name: VDIF
dependent_variable.definition: Percentage difference between the analysts’ accounting-based equity value estimate and share price: VDIF=(AV−P)/P. AV is book value plus discounted expected abnormal earnings for years 1–4 and a terminal abnormal-earnings term at year 5. Mean analyst EPS forecasts supply t+1 and t+2; for t+3 through t+5 expected EPS uses the mean long-term growth forecast times prior-year EPS. Expected book value rolls forward prior book value plus expected EPS less expected dividends; expected dividends equal expected EPS times PAYOUT. PAYOUT averages the prior three years’ dividend-to-net-income ratio; for this calculation, negative net income is set to 6% of total assets. Cost of equity is the greater of the market-model return estimate and the 10-year Treasury rate; negative AV is set to zero. The supplied reading text has a corrupted summation glyph in the printed A1 value formula; the candidate transcription is documented in the worker report and remains unverified.

evidence.quote: Specifically, we first set VDIF = ( AVt  - Pt ) /Pt, where Pt is share price and
E t ( EPSt + i ) equals time t mean analyst forecast of earnings per share for year t + i, for i = 1 , 2.
Thus, we set E t ( EPSt + i ) equal to the time t mean analyst long-term earnings growth forecast times EPSt + i −1, for i = 3 through 5.
E t ( BVE t + i ) equals BVE t + i −1 + E t ( EPSt + i ) − E t ( DIVt + i ), where DIVt is dividends in year t .
We set E t ( DIVt + i ) equal to E t ( EPSt + i ) × PAYOUT, where PAYOUT is the firm’s dividend payout ratio.

The firm’s cost of equity capital, r, equals the greater of R f + β ( Rm - R f ) or R f, where β is estimated from the market model, R f is the 10-year Treasury Bill rate, and ( Rm - R f ) is 7.6%, following Ibbotson Associates [1996].
If AVt is negative, we set it to zero.

We define the dividend payout ratio as the average of the prior three years ratio of dividends-to-net income. Consistent with Frankel and Lee [1998], among others, if net income in a particular year is negative, for purposes of this calculation, we set it equal to 6% of total assets.
